lesson.title: Splitting the Difference: The Voltage Divider Circuit
lesson.summary: Derives the voltage divider formula from Ohm's law and series circuit behavior, works a numeric example, and explains the loading effect that arises when a real load is connected to the output.
lesson.body:
A voltage divider is one of the most useful and most frequently encountered small circuits in all of electronics, and it is built from nothing more than two resistors in series, which you already know how to analyze. The idea is simple: since a shared current flows through both resistors and each drops a voltage proportional to its own resistance, tapping a wire off the junction between the two resistors gives you an output voltage that is some predictable fraction of the total input voltage, a fraction set entirely by the ratio of the two resistances.

The derivation follows directly from what you already know. With R1 and R2 in series across input voltage Vin, the current through both is I = Vin / (R1 + R2). The output voltage, taken across R2, is Vout = I times R2 by Ohm's law, and substituting the expression for I gives the voltage divider formula, Vout = Vin times R2 / (R1 + R2). Notice that Vout depends only on the ratio of R2 to the total resistance, not on the absolute size of either resistor, which is why voltage dividers can be built from resistors of very different magnitudes as long as their ratio is correct.

Suppose you have a 5 volt input and want roughly one third of that voltage at the output. Choose R1 = 1000 ohms and R2 = 2000 ohms. The output is Vout = 5 times 2000 / (1000 + 2000) = 5 times 2000/3000, which equals approximately 3.33 volts. Notice that R2, the resistor across which you are measuring, is the one that appears in the numerator, a detail that trips up many beginners who write the formula with the wrong resistor on top.

There is an important catch, though, and it becomes relevant the moment you connect anything to the divider's output that draws current, such as a sensor or the input of another circuit stage. That load resistor effectively sits in parallel with R2, exactly the kind of series parallel combination covered in the previous section, and it pulls the effective resistance at that node down, which reduces the output voltage below the value predicted by the simple two resistor formula. This behavior is called the loading effect, and it is why voltage dividers used to supply real loads are typically designed with resistances much smaller than the load they are feeding, or are buffered by an amplifier stage instead.

Despite that limitation, voltage dividers remain everywhere in practical circuits: setting bias voltages for transistors, scaling a large sensor voltage down into a range a microcontroller's analog input can safely read, and forming the basis of potentiometers, which are really just voltage dividers with a mechanically adjustable tap point instead of a fixed resistor ratio. Mastering this one small circuit pays off across an enormous range of later topics.

It is also worth noticing what the divider formula predicts at its extremes, since checking limiting cases is a habit that catches algebra mistakes early. If R2 is made much larger than R1, the ratio R2 / (R1 + R2) approaches 1, and Vout approaches the full input voltage, which makes sense because almost all of the voltage drop concentrates across the much larger resistor. If R2 instead shrinks toward zero, Vout approaches zero as well, since a vanishingly small resistance can only support a vanishingly small voltage drop for any finite current. Both extremes match physical intuition, which is a good sign the formula itself is trustworthy.
